query: Starting from an as-processed Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy with a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution-plus-intermetallic state and a target density below 6 g/cm3, what single intervention could overcome performance limitations associated with stable intermetallic formation while improving room-temperature compressive behavior, corrosion resistance, and resistance to high-temperature oxidation? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts measurable changes relative to the as-processed baseline, defines the relevant composition, temperature, exposure-time, and test-environment boundaries, cites supporting evidence from previously reported Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys, and proposes a controlled experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying high pressure and high temperature (HPHT) to the Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy can overcome performance limitations associated with stable intermetallic formation while improving room-temperature compressive behavior, corrosion resistance, and resistance to high-temperature oxidation.
generation.intervention: High pressure and high temperature (HPHT) treatment
generation.conditions: Target density below 6 g/cm3, room temperature, and high-temperature oxidation environment
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a single-phase face-centered cubic (SP-FCC) structure
generation.mechanism: Derived from materials-science principles, the HPHT treatment can promote the transition from intermetallic compounds to solid solutions, leading to improved mechanical and corrosion properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved room-temperature compressive behavior, corrosion resistance, and resistance to high-temperature oxidation

falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HPHT-treated samples do not show improved mechanical and corrosion properties compared to the as-processed samples, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: In this work, we developed a low-density (2.4 g/cm3) and high specific yield strength (344 × 103 N·m/kg) Al55Mg35Li5Zn5 CCA with a single-phase face-centered cubic (SP-FCC) structure by applying high pressure and high temperature (HPHT) to promote the transition from IMCs to solid solutions. The formation of the SP-FCC lattice is attributed to the decreased differences in atomic size and electronegativity between the solute elements and Al under high pressure, as well as the synergistic high entropy effect caused by high temperature and high pressure. The distinct solid solution strengthening comes from the incorporation of multiple elements in one single FCC lattice, as well as the significant pinning effect of dislocations from nanoscale chemical fluctuations, which leads to the enhanced strength of the low-density CCA.

This study provides new perspectives and a new understanding of the oxidation and corrosion behaviors of high-entropy alloys, revealing their outstanding performance during the oxidation process. With the development of materials science, high-entropy alloys, as a novel material, possess great potential in industrial applications due to their superior mechanical properties, high-temperature resistance, and corrosion resistance. In the future, with continuous research, it is expected that high-entropy alloys will be widely applied in various fields such as aerospace, energy, chemical engineering, and automotive manufacturing. Especially in high-temperature, high-pressure, and extreme environments, they are expected to become important structural and functional materials.

Complex concentrated alloys (CCA) represent a new group of materials, with complex microstructures, comprising of a large number of elements []. CCAs extend the established limits of the high entropy alloys (HEAs) concept by allowing a smaller number of elements in the composition and in various proportions, that can deliver mixed structures containing solid solution and well dispersed intermetallic phases. CCAs generally have higher configurational entropy than conventional alloys and are capable of obtaining complex, disordered compositionally complex solid solution structures. CCAs are distinct from conventional alloys in that they are not based on a single major element and rather include several main elements, which allow a high degree of freedom in alloy compositions and properties. Their properties, such as high temperature resistance, corrosion resistance, workability, and low density, offer a remarkable advantage in the use of CCAs for various extreme conditions applications [,].
